utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we begin, the Prosecution will be tendering a binder with eight exhibits. If it would be possible to get a number for that exhibit now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The first exhibit, tab 1, will be P420 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've been -- the practice we've been following is simply to give one exhibit number and then we give the tabs thereafter.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So if we have 420 for the bundle and then the various tabs in it will follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if I could begin by asking the witness be shown this sheet of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Witness B-1003, I'd ask you to take a look at the sheet of paper before you and I'd ask is that your name and date of birth on that sheet of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Throughout the course of this morning you will be referred to as B-1003 to protect your identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that the pseudonym sheet be tendered into evidence under seal. It is not part of the binder so would not be in with the binder 420.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It can be a separate number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The pseudonym sheet is marked P421.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: B-1003, we are in open session at the moment. I would ask you for the extent that you can without identifying yourself, would you briefly summarise your educational and professional background.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: I graduated from a police course, a police training course, and before the war I worked as a member of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that your primary occupation has been working for the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to the spring of 1992. Did there come a time when you overheard a conversation on an official police radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe the circumstances of you hearing that conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: It was a conversation between two of my colleagues who were Serb by ethnicity, and they were talking during the time that there was a police station in a car and it was switched on so that all the employees of the Ministry of the Interior who could reach that channel were able to hear that same conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you summarise for the Court what you recall about that conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: The whole course of the conversation referred to the situation in the Republic of Croatia and the relationships that prevailed at the time, that is to say, the Serb forces in Croatia, how they were moving ahead with respect to the Croatian ones and how they cleared up, for example, Croatian defence, and that the Croatian forces were doing very badly and fared very badly and the same thing could be expected to happen in Bosnia between the Muslims and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask we go into private session for a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: B-1003, as you were entering Bijeljina on this occasion, can you describe what you observed about any military surrounding Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, I can. On that section of the road, I was stopped and there were a large number of military men, soldiers, reservists, so that they had surrounded Bijeljina. They were stationed all around Bijeljina with heavy weapons, heavy artillery, and so on. They were armed extensively.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were these official JNA troops?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: No. No, they weren't. Actually, I couldn't know because some people were wearing military uniforms, JNA uniforms, and others were in civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe the military equipment that you saw in the outskirts of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Well, of course they had all the necessary military equipment and materiel which had previously belonged to the army of Yugoslavia, all that kind of weaponry. And it had all come from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you see any artillery pieces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes. There were mortars, mortar nests with mortars, and I saw the occasional cannon, gun. Whether it was a Howitzer or whatever, a smaller gun, cannon, I can't really say which kind because I'm not that familiar with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The cannon and the mortars, were you able to see in which direction they were aimed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, I could. They were all aimed at Bijeljina, in the direction of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe your observations when you first entered the town, after you entered it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, I can. When I entered Bijeljina, while I was driving along the road towards the police station, there were many military troops there belonging to different kinds of armed forces. I wasn't able to establish their identity at that time. Some people wore the caps, pointed caps. Some were wearing camouflage uniforms or half, half, half uniform, half civilian clothing. Others were in civilian clothing in that part as I approached Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you report for work when you returned to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes. I had to report to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what is your best recollection of the date that you entered Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: 1st of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, upon returning, were police officers required to sign a document that prior to this they had not been required to sign?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: It was a document pledging loyalty to the Serb authorities or you signed to say that you were going to work for the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when non-Serbs were dismissed from certain posts within the police department?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: After that, after the signing of these documents, later on the situation became even worse. It became even more difficult to work, and there were great problems between the Muslims and the Serbs so that people were dismissed from their jobs. They would also leave of their own free will. And at the beginning of the conflict itself in Bijeljina, if you didn't report to work in the first one, two, or three days, you were automatically dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I'd ask that Prosecution Exhibit P420, tab 1, be placed on the ELMO. I'm sorry. Your Honour, just before we begin working with this exhibit, this is an exhibit drawn -- a basic map drawn by another witness. It's a photocopy of that, and that was Prosecution Exhibit 411, tab 8. This particular witness has drawn numbers on that map to indicate certain locations he will be testifying about here today, but the map is not his, it's another witness, and that was -- B-1738 is the witness who is the author of this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: B-1003, did there come a time when you became aware that that was large number of civilian corpses on the streets of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We are now in public session. Can I ask you to describe to the extent possible what you knew about these corpses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: What I can say is that they were the corpses of persons who had been killed from firearms, and their ages ranged from 10 to 70 years. And those people were predominantly or, rather, -- none of them were armed. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. They were all unarmed, wearing civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The numbers that are on the map that is on the overhead projector, do those numbers indicate the approximate locations of those civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, they do. Those are the locations roughly where the bodies were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Approximately how many bodies altogether did you become aware of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Approximately, as far as I know, 48 bodies. There were more though.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where were most -- where were those -- the 48 bodies, where were they stored?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: All the persons collected up from these locations were placed in the hospital compound in Bijeljina by the mortuary in the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you said that you believed there were more. Can you please describe what you meant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: There were quite a few bodies that were not brought to the hospital compound because their family members would take over the bodies and bury them in the Bijeljina Muslim cemetery without having other people know or having them brought into hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 420, tab 2. It is on the computer screen. I'd ask that the witness's screen be pushed to "off". I believe that's what will allow him to see it. I would draw the Chamber's attention to photograph D.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, is there a photograph displayed before you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recognise what that -- what is the location depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: I think that is one of the side entrances to the hospital which is where the mortuary is located.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you recognise the uniforms of the people depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, I do. They are members of the Serb forces. And the person up in front I think belonged to Arkan's forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would ask that the usher -- if we could leave that map on the overhead, but there's no need to stand there next to it. I would ask that we now go into private session for a few questions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, during this time period, who, if anybody, gained control over the grounds of the hospital in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: The hospital was held by the Serbian Volunteer Guards and Serbian paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recall the identity of those paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: There were different ones. There was the Serbian Volunteer Guards first, then the White Eagles, then members of the new Serbian guards who during the conflicts joined Arkan's forces, and other paramilitary groups who I'm not able to name. Anyway, they were stationed together with the others near the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During early April, did a shipment of police equipment arrive from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes. The shipment arrived consisting mostly of berets and the badges that were attached to the berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when is your best recollection with respect to when these berets and badges arrived from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: The first shipment arrived, as far as I can remember, the second evening after the conflict erupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was there an instruction given to police officers with respect to the wearing of these berets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes. It was mandatory to wear berets for personal security.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you or were you familiar at that time with the appearance of berets worn by the Serbian Ministry of Interior police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes. They were identical berets worn by the members of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were -- became aware that the police chief of Bijeljina was making regular trips to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the name of that police chief?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Predrag Jesuric.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like to ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 420, tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to take a look at the last page of that document and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. ask you do you recognise the seal that's contained on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, it is the seal of the public security station signed by Predrag Jesuric, chief of the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to now look at the first page of the document. I'm going to ask you to read the third paragraph of that document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: The public security station in Bijeljina, starting with the 1st of April, 1992. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Witness, do you have the document in your language?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, he does.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Do I have to read it aloud or for myself?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask you just a few questions from that document. Based on your personal knowledge, is paragraph 3 of this document, is it an accurate reflection of the situation as you observed it in Bijeljina at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please correct what is incorrect in this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: From the very beginning of the conflict, that is, on the 1st of April, all that is true is that there was an interruption in the reporting by the public security station to the legal bodies of MUP in Bosnia and Herzegovina, so that reporting went only to the bodies of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to the paragraph above this one, and the first sentence of that paragraph, and I'll read from the English translation. I'd ask to you look at the original document and I'm ask you a question regarding it. "Since the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina began work on the 1st of April, 1992, police station chief, Predrag Jesuric, and federal SUP secretary of interior coordinator, Petar Mihajlovic, who visited the police station on several occasions during this period have been trying to come in telephone contact with the seat of ministry and send reports but to no avail." My question to you is: Were you aware that members of the federal Ministry of interior were present in Bijeljina during the first week of April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. An inspector came from the federal SUP, federal Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At the time that that federal inspector came to Bijeljina, were you aware that his title or his position was that of coordinator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: No. No, I was not aware of that, because the federal SUP had no competency over public security stations. And if it did have any assignment for that particular police station, then the Federal Secretariat would have to go through the republic secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, what time would the Chamber like to take the morning break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we started late. Let me just confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm making inquiries to see if we can sit until 2.00 this afternoon to make up some lost time. Go on for another ten minutes and we'll break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Witness B-1003, I'd like to draw your attention to the second paragraph on the second page. I will read from the English translation of that. I'd ask you to read along in the original and I would then ask you a question. The English translation reads: The security situation in Bijeljina was destabilised at about," and the exact time is illegible, "hours on the evening of the 31st of March, 1992, when Muslim extremists put up roadblocks in the centre of town. During the night and the following day, the Territorial Defence, the Serbian National Guard and the Serbian Volunteers Guard began to lift the blockade of the town under the guidance of the Crisis Staff of Bijeljina municipality." Sir, my question to you is: This particular paragraph seems to suggest that there was an immediate response by the Serbian Volunteer Guard and the Serbian National Guard to the placement of roadblocks in the town of Bijeljina. To your knowledge, did the Serbian Volunteer Guard arrive the same night when -- as when trouble began over the roadblocks in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: As far as I know, they arrived the following day, the next day when the conflicts broke out, the incidents that took place in Bijeljina. But on the first evening, as far as I know, there weren't any special conflicts or clashes. It was just the beginning. So there was just a brief period of sporadic shooting. And then, as far as I know, at two locations, barricades were set up by the Muslim side, by the Muslim people, but they were barricades made up of one or two vehicles that made a sort of roadblock. They blocked the road. They weren't actually proper barricades in the defence sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The last phrase of this paragraph refers to the Crisis Staff of Bijeljina municipality. On the 1st of April were you aware that such an organisation existed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, the Crisis Staff did exist the whole time, and it organised everything that was going on. Everything went via the Crisis Staff, and it was located in Dvorovi at the beginning of the conflict and was then transferred to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd now ask that we go into private session for the next portion of testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, could I ask you to describe after the 1st of April, what was the relationship between Arkan's men and the local police in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: After the 1st of April, Arkan's men would enter where they were permitted to and where they weren't. They would enter the police station premises and offices. They would take the police cars without first asking. They would take documents and the weapons that had already been seized from the Muslim people, sidearms, pistols, light weapons. Anything that was nice and interesting, they would confiscate it, take it, and then they would make their own -- draw up their own licenses to carry those guns and weapons. And traffic permits, driver's licences, ID cards and everything. They could do whatever they liked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did members of Arkan's unit accompany ordinary police patrols in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: As far as I know, in the first week after the conflict had broken out, there would always be a -- the policemen would always be escorted by one of Arkan's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were police units able to patrol without the presence of Arkan's -- one of Arkan's men in the police vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: No. No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that's a convenient place to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes. Witness B-1003, don't speak to anybody, please, about your evidence until it's completed, and that includes members of the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: B-1003, we broke at the portion of your testimony where you were describing Arkan's men being involved in patrols. Did you yourself personally see Arkan present in the town of Bijeljina during this time period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was one of these occasions when Ms. Plavsic -- Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Abdic were also present in town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe the circumstances of you seeing Arkan on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: The first time I saw Arkan was close to the headquarters of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, we are in public session now. The first occasion, do we need to be in private session?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: The first time I saw him was not far from the Territorial Defence headquarters, and he moved around in a vehicle. And with him in the car was Mr. Zecevic. And the second time I saw him was when a delegation arrived from Sarajevo, Mrs. Plavsic, in fact, and Mr. Fikret Abdic, and that was in front of the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The first occasion that you saw him, what was the name, the first name, of Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please repeat. Please repeat his first name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Ferid. Ferid Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was his occupation, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: He was a professor at the secondary school in Bijeljina, and he also had a catering establishment in Bijeljina, it's on Racanska Cesta street.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you know if he is alive today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: No. What happened to him was that I think in July, he was killed. I think he was killed in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: July of what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The transcript reports you as saying that he died last year, 2002. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the second time you saw Arkan you described it as being during the course of this delegation which arrived in Bijeljina. My question for you is: Who provided the security for that event in Bijeljina? Was it the Bijeljina police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: No, no. The police didn't provide the security. On that occasion, there were Arkan's men deployed in the municipality building and around it, and they provided the security for the municipality. The police did not take part in escorting the vehicle or providing security for those individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, drawing your attention to the latter part of April and continuing throughout the summer of 1992, was it possible for people to leave Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: It was possible to leave Bijeljina, but only if you had authorisation or, rather, permit from the Crisis Staff. You could leave Bijeljina then and go off in any direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when you say "authorisation from the Crisis Staff," was this in the form of a document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes. You had to get -- if you wanted to leave Bijeljina or the SAO Semberija or Majevica area, you had to table a request to the Crisis Staff and then you would be issued a written piece of paper authorising you to leave the area of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were all ethnicities or people of all ethnicities able to attain this document with equal ease?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: No, it wasn't easy. You had to send in a request, and you might get it or not, especially members of the Muslim population and Croatian ethnicity. It was more difficult for them to obtain a permit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If somebody was intending to leave without having acquired this documentation, where would they be stopped or checked to see that they -- whether they had the necessary paperwork to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: At all the border crossings, the border with the Republic of Serbia. That's where the checkpoints were set up or border crossings. And in the other areas, towards other areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were also checkpoints, police checkpoints to control the comings and goings or, rather, the persons wishing to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During your time in Bijeljina after the beginning of April 1992, did you form an impression regarding who it was that was controlling or issuing directives to the Ministry of Interior of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was the ministry or, rather, the Bijeljina police station was subordinated to the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska so that they would come under that ministry, whereas everything -- all links and ties with the ministry of Bosnia-Herzegovina were severed, and they cooperated with the people from the federal SUP, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what role, if any, did Arkan play in directing the activities of the local police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: As far as I know, Arkan was linked from the very beginning of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. conflict in Bijeljina with the Crisis Staff, so that it was the Crisis Staff, together with Arkan, which gave out instructions to the police as to how to conduct its work and what the police should do and should not do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a person by the name of Mauzer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How -- how do you know him, and what was his role in the events of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was the commander of that Crisis Staff generally speaking. Everything that was going on went via him in Bijeljina and the surrounding areas, the Semberija region, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In early May, did you have an opportunity to go to the Brcko region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Chamber your observations regarding Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: The second day after the conflict had broken out in Brcko, we were sent there by the police station of Bijeljina to provide security for certain buildings and premises in Brcko, to take control of them, but we didn't know at all that there were major conflicts going on in the area. So we went to Brcko to take up our positions securing the buildings, that is to say, the post office, the municipality building, the department store, other shops, so that when we arrived, everything was already empty and there was nothing to secure. On one occasion, they tried to transfer us to the front line, but -- that is to say that the police station of Brcko asked that we be transferred to the front line. But the commander in Bijeljina refused and put us up at the Brcko hotel. So we just provided security for some small buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: While you were in Brcko, were you able to identify men from any groups that you were -- that were known to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, according to the summary I have with me, I notice that the Prosecution is asking some private session for this. If you're okay, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has been -- has told us that this particular part of his testimony is okay. I appreciate that the Chamber's caution, reminder. I'll just confirm with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Witness B-1003, is it okay for you to testify about this in open session, publicly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's okay. Would you repeat your question, please, the last question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. While you were in Brcko, were you able to identify any groups of men that were present in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: When I went to Brcko from Bijeljina, or, rather, a regular police force was sent from the Bijeljina police station to Brcko. There were some reservists of the Territorial Defence, and there were a lot of paramilitaries which accompanied those same forces. And in the town of Brcko itself, groups of Arkan's men were already there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In addition to Arkan's men, were you able to identify any other groups that these men belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Well, there were members of the White Eagles, Beli Orlovi, and members of the territorial composition, members of the reserve force of the army, army reservists. I can't really say who belonged to what, who belonged to the army and who didn't, because as I say, there were people in civilian clothes or half-half, half civilian, half uniforms. Some people with insignia and patches and so on, others without. The members of the White Eagles had their badges, so I was able to recognise them as I was able to recognise members of Arkan's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention now to -- I'm going to ask you to take a look at a photograph in front of you, and I would ask that we go into private session for this particular photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: B-1003, during the period after beginning of April 1992, did you become aware that lists were being used by the police to check for, or to identify, particular Muslims in the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes. Every police checkpoint at the exits from SAO Semberija had this list of Muslims who needed to be taken into custody or arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you yourself have an opportunity to see this list on at least one occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, I did have one occasion to see that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe what you recall about the names on that list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: The list was of Muslims, people of Muslim ethnicity, who were mostly well-off, who had businesses of their own or who had companies of their own of some significance in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 420, tab 6. I'm going to ask that the original or a photocopy made from the original be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: B-1003, I'm going to ask you, in the first paragraph of this document there are a number of villages that are identified. I'd ask you to read those villages to us and then tell us, are you familiar with those villages and are they in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes. These are villages close to Bijeljina in the direction of Tuzla, Trnova, Glinje, Teocak, and Snijeznica and I am familiar with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, this document purports to record that the Muslim people -- population of these villages made an expression of loyalty to the new Serb authorities of Bijeljina. My question to you is: To your knowledge is this an event that did actually occur? Did the Muslim population of these villages in fact make an expression of loyalty to the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, those populations made a declaration of loyalty to Republika Srpska. And after making the declaration of loyalty in the same villages, police guards were performed which in agreement with the new Ministry of Interior of the Republic Srpska were formed and they were allowed to operate in those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there any violence in those villages as far as you can recall, or as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, no. From these villages, Trnova, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Glinje, Janjari, Atmacici, due to fear provoked by the Serbian forces around those villages because there was shooting every night around the villages, so that as far as I know, later on all these villages, the inhabitants of all these villages voluntarily moved out in the direction of Teocak.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when did that occur?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: I think it was in July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to look at the picture on the screen before you. Do you recognise the location depicted in these two photographs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: As far as I am able to see, this is the area where the mosque was across the road from the hospital in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I now ask -- now there's nothing standing here now. Was that mosque destroyed during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know, that mosque and the others were all destroyed, but not in the conflict, after the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to look at Prosecution Exhibit 420 tab 8 on the monitor in front of you. Do you recognise this location and the ruins that are there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes. I think this is also a mosque, used to be a mosque, in the village of Atmacici

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And prior to the conflict, was this mosque standing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes. There were no conflicts in this area at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you visit this site after the mosque was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you able to make observations that indicated to you how the mosque came to collapse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes. The mosque was destroyed with the help of explosives. It was mined and blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the ferry crossing at Badovinci, connecting Bijeljina to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In the spring and summer of -- or March and April of 1992, can you describe for the Chamber what would have been the border controls, if any, at that location? What would have been the regular border controls?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Regular border controls were not there. As far as the Bosnian side is concerned, a new bridge was being built across the Drina River, and before the bridge was built there was a ferry operating transporting passengers across to the other side, whereas from the other side, that is, in the Republic of Serbia, there was a regular police patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On occasion did your duties include stationing yourself on the Bosnian side of the border between Bosnia and Serbia in order to look for suspicious activity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Not there, but at other crossing points, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And at the crossing points that you had occasion to be stationed at between Bosnia and Republic of Serbia, were there border controls on the Serbian side of that border?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 326 again. It's the photocopy of the map that he's made markings on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: B-1003, I'm going to ask you to conclude your testimony here today simply by pointing to each of the locations on this map starting with A and just going alphabetically and indicate to the Chamber the significance of each of these locations. I'd ask you to call out the letter as you do so the record is clear what you're referring to. And there's a pointer there in front of you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: "A", I marked with "A" the place called Popovi. That was where the Crisis Staff was set up prior to the attack on Bijeljina, and all orders came from there. The letter "B" indicates the area where Arkan's forces were stationed, and it is there that they crossed from Serbia into the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "C", "C" and "D" are border crossings, the border crossing between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia where there were regular checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Just would ask you, "G" you've already told us about in private session, so I'd ask you to stop at "F". Please continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: I've already said that "C" and "D" were the regular checkpoints by the regular police of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Serbia and a crossing -- the bridge across the Sava. That was secured by members of the reserve force of the army which used to be the Yugoslav army and the reserve police force. "E" and "F" are places referred to in this last document, the three villages there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, it is my submission that this excessive use of private session serves only to dramatise the statement of this witness who is giving erroneous explanations in connection with the events in Bijeljina, and there's no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You begin your cross-examination. The matter of the use of private session is not really a matter for you. It's a matter for the Court which has to determine it. You know the rules. If there are matters which may in any way identify the witness, then he's entitled to a private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not mention the name of the witness, nor is it my intention to identify him, but I assume there is no secret, nor is it for a private session to say the fact that he was a policeman in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, help us with that, will you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it hasn't specifically been stated. Perhaps the witness would be the best person to ask whether he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness B-1003, if at any time you feel your security or your -- if there are any matters which you would wish to be dealt with in private session, just indicate and we can go back into private session. But obviously we should try and remain in open session as much as we.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope, Mr. May, that we will be in public session throughout because I have no intention of revealing his identity and as you see, the witness himself has agreed there is no dispute as to the work he did and the position he held, that that is no secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said on television that you saw a conflict had occurred in Bijeljina. At the time you were on assignment somewhere else; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know how the conflict in Bijeljina broke out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: As far as I know, it occurred the day before I was in Bijeljina. A conflict occurred between individual groups of Muslim ethnicity and groups of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. There's no dispute over that. But my question is how the conflict actually occurred. Is it true that Green Berets and the forces of the so-called League had blocked Bijeljina and set up barricades in many places in Bijeljina and taken up positions and established firing positions in various places in Bijeljina? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no barricades. If I -- if there were, I would have seen them. I know of one or, rather, two. At the entry to Bijeljina and around Bijeljina, there were barricades held by Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, as that is your explanation, explain this for me, please: A moment ago and also on page 2, paragraph 4, you say that Bijeljina was surrounded by a water armour, something like that. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Bijeljina -- around Bijeljina there was a canal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Come now. The inhabitants of Bijeljina are watching us. Isn't it true that only a small canal goes through Bijeljina called Dasnica? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that canal passes right by the police station; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that canal has been in existence for decades, anyways, since before you were born; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No canal or trench filled with water ever existed, nor is there such a thing around Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: I'd like you to go and visit and see for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there were canals filled with water around Bijeljina? Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that Bijeljina was surrounded by the JNA. Is that what you're claiming, indeed, or is it an assumption of yours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that Bijeljina was surrounded by JNA forces but that civilians, paramilitary units that were in the area around Bijeljina, they were armed with JNA weapons. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean with JNA weapons? You mean with the same kind of weapons that the JNA had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you don't know the source of those weapons, nor are you claiming that they were given them by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Yugoslav army had all weapons of Yugoslav manufacture that I could recognise and that I could see, that I had occasion to see close up and which I had learnt about anyway serving in that same army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there's no dispute over that, but surely all the armies in the territory of the former Yugoslavia had the same weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't have JNA weapons, you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: What do you mean "you"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I mean, for instance, the Green Berets, the league. Didn't they have the same weapons as the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: I apologise, but I was not a member of the Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, but do you know, how long did that war in Bijeljina go on for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: About six days. Actually, there were clashes actually for the first two days, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that after that the situation calmed down and that there were no conflicts afterwards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes. The situation in the town of Bijeljina itself was peaceful for about -- about a month later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Were you in Bijeljina then? So do you know that at that time when the situation calmed down that those various members of Muslim paramilitary formations that had blocked Bijeljina handed over, surrendered more than 500 long-barrelled weapons? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: As far as I know with regard to the surrender of those weapons, as far as I know, those long-barrels that were handed over, I didn't see a single one. The rest were sidearms, pistols that people had with legally obtained licenses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But pistols are not long barrels. Do you know that the 500 long barrels were also weapons of Yugoslav make?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You do not listen. You don't listen to the reply. The reply was he knew nothing about it. What he knew about was pistols and the like which were handed over. Your assumption of the answers is quite wrong. You should listen to the answers and then take your questions from there rather than just going on as before.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. Don't worry. I won't put an incorrect question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's clear some things up so that they should be clear to me, because from what you have been saying here, everything is not quite clear. Will you please explain just one thing before we move on. On page 3 of your statement, you mention Seval Begic. So let's clear that point up, please. You say the hearse belonged to the communal enterprise and its manager was a Muslim, Seval Begic. "Seval came to the police station --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We're getting very close to an area that should be in private session. Just to advise Mr. Milosevic of that fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to speak indeterminately and not in the second person singular but I shall just refer to an undetermined person so that we don't have to go back into private session. You say, Mr. B-1003, that - and let me be unspecific again and express myself in that way - [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now answer me this: How come you were able to collect up 48 bodies when according to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Can we go into private session for an explanation perhaps? I thought it was clear what were the sensitive parts of the testimony, what were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not always very clear, I must say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But if this is a matter which may require a private session, we'll go into it out of an abundance of caution. Private session again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I hope we've cleared this up, that this does not threaten the disclosure of the witness's identity in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We were talking about that fact that on the streets of Bijeljina, 48 corpses were collected up. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know that all the official reports and information which were available at that time and are available now spoke of the fact that 38 persons were killed in total in Bijeljina, of which number 22 were Muslims, 15 were Serbs, and one -- one person was a Croat by ethnicity, that is to say, a Croatian lady. So are you aware of those facts and figures? Is that what is correct and not this figure -- this number of 48?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: What I know is the other number. I know about that other number. As to your facts and figures, I don't know where you got them from and who drew up those statistics. And if they did, it was -- the statistics must have been compiled by the Serbian side and by the Crisis Staff, and they did so to their advantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have no Crisis Staff statistics but official information which is available in Bijeljina. Now, let us please go back to the event itself and then we'll move on to discuss these persons. Is it true and correct that before the conflict there was a blockade of all the vital points in Bijeljina by the Green Berets and Patriotic League or, rather, the Muslim extremists? Is that what happened or not? Just say yes or no and we can move on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you claim that no barricades were erected and that there was no organised activity on the part of the Muslim extremists to block Bijeljina at all? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: I said as far as I know, to the best of my knowledge. I know about two. One was a truck in one place, and in another place there was a truck and a car. But any greater resistance or barricades I did not know about. I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. You did not know about them. Now, take a look at this diagram which shows precisely the barricades or, rather, the location in schematic form at Redzep's house which is where you say most of the people were killed. So take a look at this diagram. I have a copy, and could this be placed on the overhead projector and then we'll be able to comment on it together?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us where it comes from, Mr. Milosevic, from what it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a sketch, a diagram drawn up by eyewitnesses in Bijeljina, and the witness can either affirm or refute it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you have the diagram of the crossroads, the main street. Across the road is the hospital yard. Could this be shown on the overhead, please. We see Redzep's house. Now, what has been drawn in as being buildings and streets and the distribution of buildings and streets, is that correct, Mr. B-1003? Does it correspond to the truth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: No, the order of the houses is not the right one. This barricade wasn't here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear you what did you say about the barricade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: This barricade here the one you see on the screen, it wasn't here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where was it then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: It was in between this street and that street. That's where a truck was parked blocking the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean it was just further back several metres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: No, it couldn't have fitted in there. You couldn't have fit a truck sideways across that area there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's clarify this. Could you point again to where the barricade was or where the truck was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So a little more northerly than is indicated on the diagram?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, the truck blocked both streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is Redzep's house the one that has been drawn in as Redzep's house? Point to it, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: This is where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. So that's Redzep's house and the barricade next to Redzep's house. Now, tell me this. Apart from the house, was there a sniper's nest at the barricade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: How do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Machine-gun nest. I apologise. Precisely where Redzep's house is located.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: You mean on the ground or up on the house?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I mean on the ground. Take a look at this photograph and then you'll be able to see whether this is a machine-gun nest beside Redzep's house or not, because you say there was just a truck parked sideways, horizontally.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: I don't think this fortification, such good fortification was a machine-gun nest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it in the location you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: I'm sure you can recognise this area being an inhabitant of Bijeljina yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. And these sandbags --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Where is this, please, Witness B-1003? Where is it supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is in front of Redzep's house. I'm not 100 per cent sure, but I think it is there. On the main road, the JNA road as it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, the positioning of barricades and blocking important places in Bijeljina, not to mention the silo, the water tower, the bunker in the park, and where various other locations set up by Muslim extremists, did this precede the conflict between Serbs and Muslims or, rather, between Serb and Muslim forces in Bijeljina? Is that right or not, Mr. B-1003?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you should -- before you answer that, we'll consider the question. It's suggested, it seems to be, that there was a barricade or a blocking of the silo and the water tower and the bunker - it's not explained how this was done, but let us take it as a question - it's said by Muslim extremists or indeed any other Muslim forces. Were those buildings in any way blocked or barricaded during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, the very beginning of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The usher can take a seat. That you can leave. Just take a seat yourself. Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some facilities at the very beginning, all I can say is that I know about it but I wasn't there at the time. I didn't see it with my own eyes, so I don't know exactly, 100 per cent, that some facilities were captured by certain people of Muslim ethnicity, were occupied by them. But this was short-lived, and afterwards, the Serbian forces took over everything. Regarding the water tower, as far as I know, I know there was shooting around it. Now that there was a machine-gun nest there or not, I can't say anything about that or not because I don't know. I don't know also regarding this question of a bunker. What do you mean about the bunker?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There was a bunker in the park.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: I don't know that. I never saw anything in the park.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's leave it at that. So there were blockades there, but very quickly the Serbian forces took them over. Is that what you're claiming now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: I'm saying again, and once again that there were blockades. I know of these two places, that there was some shooting around there, I do know. But that there were any important blockades and considerable resistance, in view of such a well-fortified nest, you could easily get killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But we're not going into military tactical issues. You were saying that the Serbs took over positions that had been occupied whereby Bijeljina was blocked. Is that in dispute or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: What do you mean Bijeljina was blocked, when all of this was in the centre of town? If Bijeljina was to be blocked, it was to be blocked at the entry and exit points.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was also blocked at the exit points, and it was also blocked in various places in the centre of town. The only approaches were from Dvorovi. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: I'm pointing out once again that I didn't come across these barricades. I didn't see them except the two that I have already mentioned which are in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you're claiming that most people were killed at that location next to Redzep's house. And we've already established that there was a barricade there and there was fighting there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's not what he said. That's not what he said at all. You're misrepresenting the evidence again. I'm going to -- I'm going to ask a question. I want something clarified at the moment. What the accused seems to be putting, Witness B-1003, is that this town was taken over by the Muslims first and that the Serb forces reacted and that there was fighting and, no doubt, he says in that fighting people were killed. Now, I want to understand the position. Is that the picture or is it the picture that the Serb forces took over the town, there was some resistance and then people were killed? Can you just paint the picture for us so we can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, Serb forces surrounded Bijeljina and then they started entering Bijeljina, the Serb forces, when certain small groups, as far as I know, small Muslim groups, resisted, put up some resistance. This resistance was not very strong because no heavy weapons were used such as, for instance, higher-calibre weapons, except for the Serb forces who were shooting at that same tower. Now, whether there was someone up there on that tower, I don't know. In the area around the tower, there were no dead, as far as I know. And around this barricade, right next to this barricade, there were no dead, but in a side street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Where the dead where was in the immediate vicinity of that barricade, isn't it? The barricade at Redzep's house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, it is in the immediate vicinity. But these were elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, let's establish what it is you're claiming. There was no prior blockade or barricades erected by Muslim forces before the Serbs reacted. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: I have said what I know, and I don't know about anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what you know is -- is what you know is that there were if I was a blockade of certain points including this barricade that we analysed a moment ago by Muslim forces? Is that what happened first or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: I know only that when the Serb forces entered, the Muslim people did organise themselves slightly and put up resistance. As for barricades, I don't know. I wasn't there. I didn't see the barricades except for these two. And for me, who put up those barricades, I don't really know because I didn't find those barricades when I came there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So are you now telling us that this barricade at Redzep's house, which you are aware of -- who put up that barricade? The Serbs or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: I don't know who put it there. I know only of the truck, but who was behind it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know whether it was Serbs or Muslims who put up the barricade at Redzep's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: How I could know when I wasn't there? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who was fighting around that barricade? Was it Serbs and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: All I can answer, I have -- I wasn't there. I don't know who was fighting against whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What are you testifying about if you don't know who was fighting, where they were fighting, how they were fighting, or where they were fighting? What are you testifying about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: I have given my statement. You have it in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You say that the Serb forces were in Dvorovi; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Weren't they in Amajlije?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: That is where they came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is the distance between Dvorovi and Amajlije?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Four, five, six kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where was their headquarters in Dvorovi or Amajlije?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Initially it was at the crossing from Badovinci towards Amajlije.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who was the commander of that Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: The commander of the Crisis Staff, I think at that time, was Mauzer. I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where is Mauzer from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: He is from the area of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did Mauzer then cross over the river from Serbia or was he living there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: No. He was living in the area. But other soldiers did cross over from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean "other soldiers"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Members of Arkan's unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that they came through a private arrangement with the local leadership?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you see throughout that period anywhere the presence of the JNA? Please give me an answer to that question first.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: A couple of days later, a unit was transferred from Serbia to Bosnia. I can't tell you exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me be more specific. Did the JNA take part in those conflicts in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: In Bijeljina, no. In Janja, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Janja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There were no conflicts in Janja.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Yes, but Janja was surrounded by members of the JNA, by an armoured unit which had come from -- from Bosanska or Sremska Raca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Never mind. We have witnesses from Janja to testify about that, so I won't ask you any further questions. We will establish that easily. So the JNA did not take part in the events in Bijeljina. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: I do know that the barracks in Bijeljina did not take part. I don't know how to put it. I didn't see members coming out of the barracks. I think that between the barracks and the paramilitary troops there were many problems so that the army in the Bijeljina barracks did not interfere. I do not know that they interfered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they did not get engaged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: No. It was a communication unit so there was no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since the army did not take part, do you know whether any police from Serbia took part?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Police from Serbia? As far as I know I don't know that they took part directly. No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That would be a convenient moment. We must adjourn. We will adjourn. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of an event within these conflicts when a group of Muslim extremists from Bijeljina led by Hasan Tiric -- do you know who Hasan Tiric is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know about an event that took place when he, with a certain man called Muhamed nicknamed Musa -- do you know who Musa is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know about the event when a group of extremists, Muslim extremists, from the direction of the hospital entered into Gulja Street and in a yard there found 19-year-old Zvonko Lazarevic and asked him to say which ethnicity he belonged to? And when the man refused to say, they asked him to take his clothes off to see if he had been circumcised. And once they had established that he was in fact a Serb, he was shot with four bullets. Do you know about that event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that Mile Lukic came out of the house to see what was going on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. He doesn't know about the event, so he can't help any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about the killing of Antonija Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Take a look at these photographs, please. This is Antonija Ostojic, and this other man is Zvonko Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. He doesn't know anything about it, so there's no point showing him the photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, on the photograph is a young man who has been stripped to establish what ethnicity he was and the man he was killed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can produce these photographs in due course, but you can't do it through this witness. This witness knows nothing about these alleged events.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the witness claims that the Muslim extremists did not go around killing Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's his evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- In Bijeljina. However, this young man is -- doesn't have any weapons. Neither does this old woman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You can't prove these things through him. If you can, you can call evidence about it during your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell they this then: Do you know about the killing of Risto Stevanovic. Risto Stevanovic

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: No. I don't know the man judging by the name. I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about a man on a bicycle perhaps who was killed by snipe fire precisely at one of these strongholds held by the Muslim extremists? Could you see that in the streets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: I know about one person who was killed on a bicycle, while riding a bicycle, but what his name was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you know about the incident, would you like to take a look at this photograph of the man who was killed, who was driving his bicycle and I'm sure was not shooting at anybody while he was doing so. He was quite obviously a civilian just like the others, the other people who were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Well, I can take a look at it if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you help with that photograph at all, Witness B-1003?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I can say is that I know where this person's body was located, whereas the other person was retarded, as far as I know. Now, who shot them, I don't know. I'm not sure. This is the very centre of town at any rate. I don't know that there were Muslim snipers in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you wish to say that it was the Serbs who killed him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: I said I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can we note then that you know nothing about the killing of an elderly lady called Antonija Ostojic born in 1926?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have been through that. Now, do you want these two photographs exhibited, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. I'd like the others to be exhibited too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not exhibiting those with which the witness can't help, but you can have those two exhibited. You can have the barricade -- photograph of the barricade -- I mean not the barricade, the street exhibited which you've produced and the map which includes the barricade. You can have that exhibited too, if you wish. And we'll ask the registrar to deal with them in order beginning, perhaps, with the map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The map will be marked D57.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're further on than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 121. It should be 121 in my calculation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Okay. The map will be marked D121, and the photo will be marked D122.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And then we'll deal with the other two photographs of the dead bodies. At least they're on the same sheet, are they? That can have the next exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This photo will be marked D123.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, do you know what the name of the Croatian lady was who was also killed from the fire of Muslim extremists in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: I think her name was Milena. Whether she was Croatian and whether she was killed by Serbo-Croatian forces, I really can't say, because as far as I know about a lady who was a Croat, she was killed through the window. I don't know any details about the killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Her name was Mirjana Ilic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Possibly. I can't say. I wasn't given any names, so I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know her son, Tomislav Ilic, also a Croat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you don't know that he claims that she was killed by Muslim extremists?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How can he know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's absurd. Of course he can't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not self-evident that he doesn't know what was going on in his own town and the subject he's testifying about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about Lieutenant Smajic who died fighting against Muslim extremists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a street that had previously been called Braca Jaksic street was renamed and took his name, Admir Smajic, the second lieutenant and the -- former Second Lieutenant of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1003
utterances.text: Well, maybe he was killed on the battlefront in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
